history.answer: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter born on July 6, 1907, who became famous for her many portraits, self-portraits, and works inspired by the nature and artifacts of Mexico[1]. She belonged to the post-revolutionary Mexicayotl movement, which sought to define a Mexican identity, and was also described as a surrealist or magical realist[1][2]. Her personal life and artwork were heavily influenced by the Mexicanidad movement, which seeks to revitalize the culture of Mexico's indigenous peoples[2]. She used self-portraits as a therapeutic way to express her anguish and pain, and she reclaimed her body from medical issues and gender conformity[3]. Kahlo is also known for painting about her experience of chronic pain[1].

top.text: Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón (; 6 July 1907 – 13 July 1954) was a Mexican painter known for her many portraits, self-portraits, and works inspired by the nature and artifacts of Mexico. Inspired by the country's popular culture, she employed a naïve folk art style to explore questions of identity, postcolonialism, gender, class, and race in Mexican society. Her paintings often had strong autobiographical elements and mixed realism with fantasy. In addition to belonging to the post-revolutionary Mexicayotl movement, which sought to define a Mexican identity, Kahlo has been described as a surrealist or magical realist. She is also known for painting about her experience of chronic pain. Her 1940 self-portrait titled The Dream (The Bed) holds the record for the most expensive work by a female artist ever auctioned, at $54.7 million.

Four nations have "Amazonas" as the name of one of their first-level administrative regions, and France uses the name "Guiana Amazonian Park" for French Guiana's protected rainforest area. Alexander Graham Bell (; born Alexander Bell; March 3, 1847 – August 2, 1922) was a  Scottish-born Canadian-American inventor, scientist, and engineer who is credited with patenting the first practical telephone. He also co-founded the American Telephone and Telegraph Company (AT&T) in 1885.
Bell's father, grandfather, and brother had all been associated with work on elocution and speech, and both his mother and wife were deaf, profoundly influencing Bell's life's work. His research on hearing and speech further led him to experiment with hearing devices, which eventually culminated in his being awarded the first U.S. patent for the telephone, on March 7, 1876. Bell considered his invention an intrusion on his real work as a scientist and refused to have a telephone in his study.

history.answer: The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed, crowned woman on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. It was dedicated on October 28, 1886, and was created by sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with the help of Richard Morris Hunt and Gustave Eiffel[1][5]. The statue is inspired by the Roman goddess of liberty, Libertas, and stands as a symbol of American freedom[1][3]. It is a National Historic Landmark and a World Heritage Site, recognized for its cultural and historical significance[5].

The Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World; ) is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed and crowned woman on Liberty Island, part of New York City, in New York Harbor. The copper-clad statue, a gift to the United States from the people of France, was designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, and its metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel. The statue was dedicated on October 28, 1886.
The statue is a figure of a classically draped woman, inspired by the Roman goddess of liberty, Libertas. She holds a torch above her head with her right hand, and in her left hand carries a tabula ansata inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI (July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals), the date of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. With her left foot she steps on a broken chain and shackle, commemorating the national abolition of slavery following the American Civil War.

Its most notable feature is the Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World), a large statue by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi that was dedicated in 1886. The island also contains the Statue of Liberty Museum, which opened in 2019, and exhibits the statue's original torch, which was carried by Liberty from 1886 to 1984.

top.text:
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor. He is known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system.
Born and raised in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Tesla first studied engineering and physics in the 1870s without receiving a degree. He then gained practical experience in the early 1880s working in telephony and at Continental Edison in the new electric power industry. In 1884, he migrated to the United States, where he became a naturalized citizen. He worked for a short time at the Edison Machine Works in New York City before he struck out on his own. With the help of partners to finance and market his ideas, Tesla set up laboratories and companies in New York to develop a range of electrical and mechanical devices. His AC induction motor and related polyphase AC patents, licensed by Westinghouse Electric in 1888, earned him a considerable amount of money and became the cornerstone of the polyphase system, which Westinghouse marketed.

top.text:
Mount Kilimanjaro () is a large dormant volcano in Tanzania. It is the highest mountain in Africa and the highest free-standing mountain above sea level in the world, at 5,895 m (19,340 ft) above sea level and 4900 m (16,000 ft) above its plateau base. It is also the highest volcano in the Eastern Hemisphere and the fourth most prominent peak on Earth.
Kilimanjaro's southern and eastern slopes served as the home of the Chagga Kingdoms until their abolition in 1963 by Julius Nyerere. The origin and meaning of the name Kilimanjaro is unknown, but may mean "mountain of greatness" or "unclimbable". Although it is described in classical sources, German missionary Johannes Rebmann is credited as the first European to report the mountain's existence, in 1848. After several European attempts, Hans Meyer reached Kilimanjaro's highest summit in 1889.

Insulin is a peptide hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets in the human body. It is encoded by the insulin (INS) gene and plays a key role in regulating blood glucose levels by inhibiting glucose production and secretion by the liver[1]. Circulating insulin also affects protein synthesis in various tissues[1].

There are different types of insulin used in medical treatment, including short-acting (such as regular insulin), intermediate-acting (such as NPH insulin), and longer-acting forms like insulin glargine[2]. The human insulin protein is made up of 51 amino acids with a molecular mass of about 5808 Da[3]. Insulin was the first peptide hormone ever discovered, isolated in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best[4]. It treats both type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes[5].

top.text: Insulin (; ) is a peptide hormone produced by beta cells of the pancreatic islets encoded in humans by the insulin (INS) gene. It is the main anabolic hormone of the body. It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and protein by promoting the absorption of glucose from the blood into cells of the liver, fat, and skeletal muscles. In these tissues the absorbed glucose is converted into either glycogen, via glycogenesis, or fats (triglycerides), via lipogenesis; in the liver, glucose is converted into both. Glucose production and secretion by the liver are strongly inhibited by high concentrations of insulin in the blood. Circulating insulin also affects the synthesis of proteins in a wide variety of tissues. It is thus an anabolic hormone, promoting the conversion of small molecules in the blood into large molecules in the cells. Low insulin in the blood has the opposite effect, promoting widespread catabolism, especially of reserve body fat.

Tides are the regular rise and fall in local sea levels caused by the gravitational forces of the Moon and the Sun acting on the oceans[1][2]. The Moon's tidal forces are the primary driver, but the Sun's forces also substantially modulate them[1]. The Earth's rotation and the shape of the continents further influence how water flows[1].

During each tidal cycle, at any given place the water rises to a maximum height known as "high tide" before ebbing away again to the minimum "low tide" level[2]. As the water recedes, it uncovers more of the foreshore, also known as the intertidal zone[2]. The strip of seashore that is submerged at high tide and exposed at low tide is an important ecological product of ocean tides[3].

The gravitational forces cause the entire Earth's surface to shift, including the solid crust, in response to lunar and solar gravitation[4][5]. Ocean tides produce oscillating currents known as tidal streams[3]. The responses of solid Earth to these forces are quite different from those of the oceans, even though they share the same gravitational source[4].

Tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level driven primarily by the Moon's gravitational pull, with the Sun's forces also playing a significant modulating role[1][4]. The Moon's gravity creates two bulges in the Earth's oceans: one on the side facing the Moon and another on the opposite side. As the Earth rotates, these bulges move, producing high tides and low tides approximately twice a day[3][5].

The timing and magnitude of tides vary widely across the Earth because of the continents, ocean basin geometry, bathymetry, and the Coriolis effect[1]. The water receding during low tide exposes more of the foreshore, also known as the intertidal zone[1]. Tidal energy is extracted from these periodic changes in sea levels caused by the gravitational attraction of celestial bodies[2].

Plants grow from the tips of roots and shoots through primary growth, which lengthens their stems and roots[2]. This growth is driven by meristem cells that develop into all other plant tissues and organs[2]. The process is also influenced by the plant's genome interacting with its environment, and plants can tolerate physical and biotic stresses like frost and dehydration[3].

Plants reproduce asexually by growing structures that can form new plants. For example, mosses and liverworts can be broken into pieces that regrow, and some non-flowering plants produce gemmae, small clumps of cells that detach and grow[1]. Vascular plants have two organ systems: a shoot system and a root system. The root system anchors the plant, absorbs water and minerals, and sends nutrients to the rest of the plant[4].

Trees, a type of plant, grow tall to compete for sunlight and have thickened stems with specialized cells that provide structural strength[5].

Plants are the eukaryotic organisms that constitute the kingdom Plantae . They are predominantly photosynthetic or came from photosynthetic ancestors, meaning that they obtain their energy from sunlight by using the green pigment chlorophyll in their chloroplasts to produce sugars from carbon dioxide and water. Over the course of time, some plants have evolved to be parasitic, meaning they take energy from other organisms. Except for glaucophytes, some green algae and a few red algae, most plants are multicellular.
Historically, as in Aristotle's biology, the plant kingdom encompassed all living things that were not animals, and included algae and fungi. Definitions have narrowed since then; current definitions exclude fungi and some of the algae. By the definition used in this article, plants form the clade Viridiplantae (green plants), which consists of the green algae and the embryophytes or land plants (hornworts, liverworts, mosses, lycophytes, ferns, conifers and other gymnosperms, and flowering plants). A definition based on genomes includes the Viridiplantae, along with the red algae and the glaucophytes, in the clade Archaeplastida.

It consists of two polynucleotide chains that coil around each other to form a double helix[3]. The sequence of these nucleotides along the DNA chain encodes genetic information, and genes are stretches of this sequence[2].

During cell division, DNA replication ensures that each newly divided daughter cell receives its own complete copy of each DNA molecule[4]. The two strands of double-stranded DNA are held together by base pairing rules: adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine[3]. Within cells, DNA is organised into long structures called chromosomes, and during replication, these chromosomes are duplicated to provide each cell with its own complete set of chromosomes[3]. Eukaryotes store most of their DNA inside the cell nucleus[3].

answer: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes active from the 2nd century BCE to the mid-15th century, connecting Central, East, South, Southeast, and West Asia, as well as East Africa and Southern Europe[1]. It was shaped by major events like the Black Death and Mongol conquests, and it saw immense political variation across the continent[1]. Few individuals traveled the entire length, relying instead on middlemen at stopping points along the way[1]. The route linked the civilizations of China, India, Ancient Egypt, Persia, Arabia, and Ancient Rome[2]. In later centuries, as sea trade grew, land routes like the Silk Road declined, but it still survived and expanded[2]. In the 21st century, the name "New Silk Road" describes large infrastructure projects such as the Eurasian Land Bridge and the Chinese Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)[3]. top.text: The Silk Road was utilized over a period that saw immense political variation across the continent, exemplified by major events such as the Black Death and the Mongol conquests. The network was highly decentralized, and security was sparse: travelers faced constant threats of banditry and nomadic raiders, and long expanses of inhospitable terrain. Few individuals traveled the entire length of the Silk Road, instead relying on a succession of middlemen based at various stopping points along the way. In addition to goods, the network facilitated an unprecedented exchange of religious (especially Buddhist), philosophical, and scientific thought, much of which was syncretised by societies along the way. Likewise, a wide variety of people used the routes. Diseases such as plague also spread along the Silk Road, possibly contributing to the Black Death.

Dolphins are marine mammals, not fish, and they are far larger than sharks. Dolphins are warm-blooded, breathe air through a blowhole, and give live birth, while sharks are cold-blooded fish that lay eggs or give live birth but do not breathe air[1].

Dolphins are generally smaller than most sharks, though some species like the orca can be quite large. The largest shark, the whale shark, is still much smaller than the largest dolphin, the sperm whale dolphin or orca[1].

Dolphins are active predators that feed on fish and squid, while sharks are also carnivorous but tend to eat smaller prey such as fish and other marine animals[1].

Dolphins have a blowhole and breathe air at the surface, while sharks have gills and must keep water over their gills to extract oxygen[1].

Dolphins are mammals; sharks are fish. This is the fundamental biological difference[1].

answer: The American Revolution (1765–1783) and the French Revolution (1789–1799) were both political movements that reshaped their respective societies, but they differed in scope and focus. The American Revolution was primarily a struggle for independence from British colonial rule, resulting in the creation of the United States[1][2]. The French Revolution, by contrast, aimed at a thorough overhaul of French society, including dismantling the monarchy and establishing a republic[1][4]. The American Revolution began earlier (1765) and was driven by colonial grievances, while the French Revolution started later (1789) and was marked by more violent polarization and ideological conflict between left and right[3]. Both revolutions had lasting impacts on modern democracy and political thought, but the American Revolution focused on freedom from external domination, whereas the French Revolution targeted internal social and economic structures[4].

The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799. Many of the revolution's ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, and its values remain central to modern French political discourse. It was caused by a combination of social, political, and economic factors which the existing regime proved unable to manage.
Financial crisis and widespread social distress led to the convocation of the Estates General in May 1789, its first meeting since 1614. The representatives of the Third Estate broke away and re-constituted themselves as a National Assembly in June. The Storming of the Bastille in Paris on 14 July led to a series of radical measures by the Assembly, including the abolition of feudalism, state control over the Catholic Church in France, and issuing the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

Its 16 constituent states have a total population of over 83 million, making it the most populous member state of the European Union (EU). Germany borders Denmark to the north; Poland and the Czech Republic to the east; Austria and Switzerland to the south; and France, Luxembourg, Belgium, and the Netherlands to the west. The nation's capital and most populous city is Berlin and its main financial centre is Frankfurt; the largest urban area is the Ruhr.

segments.Text: Yes, Austrian German is different from German in Germany.
Austrian German is a distinct variety of Standard German spoken in Austria and South Tyrol, with its own vocabulary and expressions.
For example, Austrians use "Jänner" for January instead of "Januar," "Feber" for February, and "heuer" for this year.
The dialectology community has debated and defended the distinction since the 1970s.
While both are varieties of German, they are not interchangeable.

history.answer: The internet is a global network of computer networks that exchange data using a shared set of rules, the Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP). Data is split into small packets, each labeled with the address of its destination. Routers pass the packets from network to network until they reach that address, where they are put back together; packets from one message may take different paths. Every device on the internet has an IP address, and the Domain Name System (DNS) translates names such as wikipedia.org into these addresses. Internet service providers connect homes and businesses, and they are linked by high-capacity backbone cables, including undersea fiber-optic cables. Services such as the World Wide Web and email run on top of this network.

history.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria turn light energy into chemical energy. In plants it takes place mainly in the leaves, inside chloroplasts that contain the green pigment chlorophyll. In the light-dependent reactions, chlorophyll absorbs sunlight, and the energy is used to split water molecules, which releases oxygen and produces the energy carriers ATP and NADPH. In the Calvin cycle, the plant uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide from the air into sugars such as glucose. The overall reaction turns six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water into one molecule of glucose and six of oxygen. Photosynthesis supplies most of the oxygen in the air and the energy for nearly all food chains.

answer:
Photosynthesis is how plants, algae, and some bacteria use sunlight to make their own food. The process takes place inside the leaves, in tiny parts called chloroplasts that contain a green pigment called chlorophyll. The plant absorbs light from the sun and uses it to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, which gives the plant energy to grow. Oxygen is released as a byproduct of this process[1][4].

The history of photosynthesis shows that scientists first discovered how the chemistry works, for example by studying bacteria that use light to convert hydrogen and carbon dioxide[2]. Over time, the process evolved from simple forms of photosynthesis in ancient organisms to the more efficient oxygen-producing photosynthesis used by plants today[5]. The overall chemical equation for the process is: light energy + water + carbon dioxide → sugar + oxygen[4].

top.text: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy—typically from sunlight—into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism. The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting. Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds (complex compounds containing carbon), typically carbohydrates like sugars (mainly glucose, fructose and sucrose), starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose. When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration. Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.

history.query: What caused the fall of the Roman Empire?
history.answer: Historians name many causes for the fall of the Western Roman Empire, which is usually dated to 476, when the last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer. Politically, the empire suffered from civil wars, frequent coups and weak emperors, especially during the crisis of the third century. Economically, heavy taxes, inflation from debased coins and shrinking trade weakened it. The army relied more and more on Germanic soldiers and allies whose loyalty was uncertain. From the late fourth century, migrating peoples such as the Goths, Vandals and Huns put pressure on the borders, and the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410. The split of the empire into eastern and western halves also left the poorer West to defend itself, while the Eastern Empire survived until 1453.

history.answer: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape once it passes the boundary called the event horizon. Black holes form when very massive stars collapse at the end of their lives, and supermassive black holes with millions to billions of solar masses sit at the centres of most large galaxies, including the Milky Way. A black hole cannot be seen directly, but astronomers detect it from its effects: the orbits of nearby stars, the glowing disk of hot gas that spirals into it, and gravitational waves when two black holes merge. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87.

history.query: How does a nuclear reactor work?
history.answer: A nuclear reactor produces heat by splitting atoms in a controlled chain reaction. The fuel is usually uranium enriched in uranium-235, formed into pellets and packed into fuel rods. When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it splits into smaller nuclei, releases a large amount of energy as heat, and frees two or three more neutrons that can split other nuclei. A moderator, often water, slows the neutrons so they cause more fissions, and control rods made of neutron-absorbing materials such as boron are moved in or out to keep the reaction steady. The heat boils water, directly or through a heat exchanger, and the steam spins a turbine connected to a generator. Thick shielding and a containment building keep the radiation inside.

answer:
A nuclear reactor works by splitting atoms in a controlled chain reaction to produce heat. This heat is then used to generate electricity.

The fuel, usually uranium enriched in uranium-235, is made into pellets and packed into fuel rods. When the atoms split, they release energy and free neutrons, which keep the chain reaction going at a controlled rate[4]. The heat from this fission is passed to a working fluid, such as water, which then drives turbines and generates electricity[3].

top.text:
A nuclear reactor is a device used to sustain a controlled fission nuclear chain reaction. They are used for commercial electricity, marine propulsion, weapons production, and research. Fissile nuclei (primarily uranium-235 or plutonium-239) absorb single neutrons and split, releasing energy and multiple neutrons, which can induce further fission. Reactors stabilize this, regulating neutron absorbers and moderators in the core. Fuel efficiency is exceptionally high; low-enriched uranium is 120,000 times more energy-dense than coal.
Heat from nuclear fission is passed to a working fluid coolant. In commercial reactors, this drives turbines and electrical generator shafts. Some reactors are used for district heating, and isotope production for medical and industrial use.

history.answer: The United Nations is an international organization founded in 1945, after the Second World War, to maintain international peace and security and to promote cooperation between countries. It has 193 member states. Its main bodies include the General Assembly, where every member has a vote, and the Security Council, whose five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, can veto its resolutions. The Secretariat, led by the Secretary-General, runs its daily work, and the International Court of Justice settles disputes between states. Its headquarters are in New York City. Specialized agencies and programmes, such as the World Health Organization and UNICEF, work on health, food, children, refugees and development.

answer: The United Nations (UN) is an international organization founded in 1945 after World War II to maintain peace and promote cooperation between countries. It has 193 member states and currently runs 11 peacekeeping missions in places like the Middle East, Kashmir, and Cyprus[1][2]. The UN Charter sets out its purposes and structure, including the General Assembly, Security Council, and other principal organs[3]. In short, the UN is a global body that works to keep the world at peace and help countries develop together.

The United Nations (UN) is an international intergovernmental organization established by the signing of the Charter of the United Nations on 26 June 1945 with the articulated mission of maintaining international peace and security, to develop friendly relations among states, to promote international cooperation, and to serve as a centre for harmonizing the actions of states in achieving those goals.
The United Nations headquarters is located in New York City, with several other offices located in Geneva, Nairobi, Vienna and The Hague. The UN comprises six principal organizations: General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, International Court of Justice, Secretariat and Trusteeship Council which, together with several specialized agencies and related agencies, make up the UN System. There is a total of 193 member states, representing nearly all of the world's sovereign states, as well as two observer states, the Holy See and the State of Palestine.
